My brain does not compute how that works for mounting your coil haha. I guess I'll have to wait for building videos.

You end up with one ascending lead and one descending lead. So what you do is:

1) Wrap your coil and leave long leads.

2) Wick your coil and feed the ascending lead through the hole towards the top of the coil.

3) Cut your wick, and feed the coil further.

4) Mount the ascending lead by screwing in the grub screw in the body of the coil. The whole body of the atty is used as the ground, rather than having two legs poking down in a standard coil rebuild. That's why I think it's so dang smart.

5) There's a grub screw and a lead hole in the positive contact, so you feed your wire through there and secure it with the grub screw to complete the circuit.

6) Trim your wires, fiddle with the wicking, and you're good to go!

The leads feed out 180* from each other, which is a super clever use of space. I think they could even reduce the size of the chamber, as well. This is also usable for vertical coil schemes, so I'm interested in seeing the first build like that come out.

I have a .375 H&H Mag. built on a Czech Mauser magnum action. (Now before you purists turn up your noses collectively I would like to remind you that the Skoda works in Czechoslovakia were world famous for their weapons)

The Mauser action is noted for Twin locking lugs at the forward end of the bolt and a Claw extractor for positive cartridge control. In fact the Mauser can be operated up side down with and the bullet will still feed correctly from the magazine into the chamber.

The Montana Rifle Company uses a Mauser type action with an integral claw type extractor for control feeding. I don't know if it is a cast or forged receiver but from their catalog they are spendy.. The other American vendors Remington, Ruger who also build .375 H&H cal use cast receivers and a spring loaded extractor (Like the AR-15 bolt). Savage makes a model 116SE in .375 H&H (SE means Safari Express) However it is also a cast receiver. I believe that the US Repeating arms Company (now hold trademark for Winchester also uses Cast Receivers. (From what I have read the cast receiver with modern casting techniques may be just as strong as a forged receiver. HOW EVER I really don't believe it for a second. Forging compresses the crystalline molecular grain structure while casting does not. For my money I would check out he CZ550. It is a very highly thought of rifle.

Here is a review from a independent Gunstore owner in Texas:> Darin Peterson, the owner of The Armory in Mesquite, Texas (972-285-1288), was kind to provide some comments on the current production CZ rifles. First, he notes that CZ rifles are the most widely used brand of rifle in Africa. Second, he states that every CZ Safari magnum that has passed through his store has had beautiful wood, a flawless, smooth action, and outstanding accuracy. He also noted that the rifle is intended to be used with the express iron sights, but it is not uncomfortable to shoot with a scope installed. CZ also offers an American style stock that is just like a Winchester or Remington. As for the trigger, out of the box the single set trigger is usually a bit squishy and heavy, and while the trigger is a bit complicated to adjust, it is fully adjustable for weight of pull, over travel, and take up. The adjustments apply to both the set trigger and standard trigger (you don't have to use the set trigger). CZ rifles also now come with swivel studs and not permanent swivels.
